title: LIVE UPDATES: Bay Area prepares for Level 2 storm; rain, winds and dangerous surf in forecast
text:
LIVE UPDATES: Level 2 storm making way to Bay Area with rain, winds and dangerous high surf in forecast - ABC7 San Francisco 
 24/7 Live San Francisco East Bay South Bay Peninsula North Bay Live WEATHER 
 LIVE UPDATES: Bay Area prepares for Level 2 storm; rain, winds and dangerous surf in forecast 
 Stream local breaking news and original programming, live 24/7, from ABC7 Bay Area. By ABC7 Bay Area Digital Staff Last updated: Friday, November 13, 2026 7:44AM GMT Share Rain is expected to return to the Bay Area on Friday, bringing gusty winds, dangerous surf and the first accumulating snowstorm of the season to the Sierra.
 ABC7 meteorologist Drew Tuma says the system has been upgraded to a Level 2 storm , the first moderate storm of the season, and is expected to bring an end to the region's fire season.
 STORM TIMELINE: Level 2 storm to bring rain, dangerous surf to Bay Area and more than a foot of snow to the Sierra 
 The heaviest rain and strongest winds are expected between 10 a.m. and 2 p.m. Friday, with showers continuing into the afternoon and a chance of thunderstorms.
 LIVE: Track rain in San Francisco Bay Area with Live Doppler 7 
 Along the coast, forecasters are warning of increasingly dangerous conditions as surf builds through Friday. A Beach Hazards Statement remains in effect through Friday afternoon, while a High Surf Warning has been issued as waves of 20 to 30 feet are expected to slam Bay Area beaches through Saturday.
 Get the latest Bay Area AccuWeather forecast here . 
 Key Headlines
 3:38 AM GMT Santa Cruz to close all beaches, wharf starting Friday night 
 Here's how the news is developing. By J.R. Stone 3 hours and 27 minutes ago 
 Mavericks could see 50-plus foot waves Saturday 
 Surfers are making their way to the coast. It's possible we could see historic waves at Mavericks in Half Moon Bay this weekend. High-surf warnings are about to go into effect along the coast.
 Santa Cruz is closing all city beaches and their wharf Friday night.
 In other areas, surfers are making their way to the coast. It's possible we could see historic waves at Mavericks in Half Moon Bay this weekend, and that has the community energized. Mavericks is a surf spot located a half-miles offshore from Pillar Point.
 "Everybody is getting their boards together making sure their fins are good, their leashes are good, hydrating, eating good!"
 "People will come here from far, from Hawaii, from East Coast," said Ricky Wong who often surfs in the harbor.
 They're coming for the big waves that have been seen along the shore, and the waves expected offshore at Mavericks. A location that has some of the largest and most gnarly waves in the world, now a large swell is headed that way.
 "Do you think we'll see 50 foot waves come Saturday?" asked ABC7 Eyewitness News reporter J.R. Stone.
 "Absolutely, absolutely the storm is out there, we've watched it form, it's pointed right at us. It's pretty exciting to know that that much energy is coming. Like when you were on the bluff today you saw big waves, it's big, it's real even today but it's going to be 2-3 times as big as today was!"
 That's Jeff Clark, surfer, Mavericks Surf Contest founder, and owner of the Mavericks Surf Company. Clark was surfing it before it became a thing.
 Others we talked with are excited about the massive waves we're expecting in the next 24 to 48 hours, but they prefer to watch.
 "Shoulder height is good enough for me. You gotta understand I'm going for the long run, not the burnout," says Wong.
 "Nah, I would not get out there on a 40-50 foot day. You gotta know your limits and that's just not something I'm ready for," said Braven Baxter who is traveling north with a friend but decided to stay to see the waves.
 Clark says his store is fully stocked with rescue vests, CO2 cartridges, wax, fins, leashes. He's already been in touch with big wave surfers from Portugal, Australia, and Hawaii.
 "You gotta have a pretty clear mind when you're stepping out there into that danger zone," said Clark.
 "You can't wipe out on that," said Stone.
 "No, and if you do it's just part of the game."
 By Tara Campbell 4:16 AM GMT 
 Oakland cleans up drains, encampments ahead of storm 
 Crews are gearing up not only for this round of rain, but also for what's expected to be a very wet El Niño winter. A storm moves into the Bay Area Friday, and crews are gearing up not only for this round of rain, but also for what's expected to be a very wet El Niño winter.
 Crews in Oakland were hard at work Thursday to prepare for the storm ahead.
 From the hills of Oakland to the low-lying streets, the is sound of the city getting prepared for the impacts of El Niño could be heard.
 Oakland Public Work crews out in full force Thursday morning making sure drains were clear ahead of Friday's forecasted rain.
 "It's very important because we expect a lot of rain this year. We need all our structures to be cleaned thoroughly. If not, we can get backups, and it can cause property damage and erosion of the streets," said Maintenance Worker Roy Luster.
 The crew pulled out everything from a grocery store basket to a sandbag that at one point was probably used to protect from flooding - now, it could be causing it.
 "Oftentimes, people use inlets as garbage, and they're not. They're for the water to flow through, so we can have easy access to the Bay," Luster said.
 And to ensure that it has a clear path to the Bay, the city is asking for the public's help.
 "The City of Oakland offers an opportunity for community members and business and local businesses to adopt a drain. So, if they have a drain in their area where debris might fall, it is a great tool for people to clean it up before a storm actually hits," said Monica Pelayo, public information officer with the Department of Public Works.
 And before the storms hit, the city's also working to clean up encampments to prevent debris from easily ending up in the drains.
 "We're clearing debris across the city. What the city is doing to reflect its values is reaching out to encampment individuals to let them know about the storm season and alternatives to being on the streets during storm season," said Liam Garland, director of Oakland Public Works. 
 By Cornell Barnard 3:38 AM GMT 
 North Bay prepares for first major storm of season 
 In the North Bay, residents are preparing for the approaching storm and trying to ease rising flood fears. In the North Bay, residents are preparing for the approaching storm and getting a helping hand from Marin County Public Works crews trying to ease rising flood fears this week.
 Marin County firefighters have been pitching in to beat the storm clock by putting a sandbag machine to good use, filling as many bags as they can.
 "We have filled a little over 30,000 sandbags since we began in October," said Marin County Public Works Assistant Director Michael Frost.
 There's no time to waste. The sandbags will be sent to neighborhoods most at risk from storm surge and king tide events.
 "We shipped out a truckload this morning. We'll do the same Friday," Frost said.
 "This is what we're doing. You can see the creek is right there. Tides are not all the way up where it could be. We're prepared for the worst," said Spencer Jackson.
 Jackson is a general contractor who is now helping Larkspur homeowners protect their waterfront homes with sandbag barriers 3 feet high around properties.
 "It's been extremely urgent for the community. We have 20 guys working 12-hour days filling up sandbags and building walls," Jackson said.
 The sound of cranes hammering steel sheets into a stormwater berm was incredibly loud, but it was music to Santa Venetia homeowners who don't want to flood again. Dennis Fiori's property flooded last January. He's concerned about approaching storms.
 "Even if we get an inch, so it will probably be OK. But if something does happen, they'll be here with sandbags immediately," Fiore said.
 Reinforcing the aging berm built in the 1980s has become a top priority for Marin County.
 "We're concerned, not only about overtopping with the berm, but also seepage underneath which is indication that it could fail," said Marin Co. Supervisor Mary Sackett.
 3:38 AM GMT 
 Santa Cruz to close all beaches, wharf starting Friday night 
 Santa Cruz will close all beaches and the Santa Cruz Wharf from 10 p.m. Friday through Sunday morning. Tomorrow's storm is expected to bring the biggest waves in years to the California coast.
 In preparation, Santa Cruz will close all beaches and the Santa Cruz Wharf from 10 p.m. Friday through Sunday 5 a.m.
 The city said in a social media post: "Please stay away from beaches, coastal access points, rocks, and other areas exposed to high surf. Large waves can arrive unexpectedly, creating life-threatening conditions even for those standing away from the water. While the Wharf remains structurally safe, these closures are being implemented as a proactive safety precaution." 
 Forecasters say breaking waves up to 30 to 40 feet are possible.
